title: Cyclic deformation behavior of a high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) magnesium alloy with heterostructures
abstract: Strain-controlled cyclic deformation behavior of a high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) Mg-1.2Zn-0.1Ca alloy fabricated via low-temperature extrusion at 150 °C was investigated at different strain amplitudes. Due to the partial dynamic recrystallization (DRX) during extrusion, the extruded HSLA magnesium alloy consisted of a unique heterostructure containing coarse unDRX grains and ultra-fine DRX grains of 0.8 µm, leading to a high tensile yield strength of 374 MPa and an elongation of 14%. The HSLA magnesium alloy exhibited cyclic stabilization at strain amplitudes of ≤0.4%, while cyclic hardening occurred at strain amplitudes of ≥0.6%. In contrast, the homogenized alloy with a uniform coarse-grained microstructure showed a strong cyclic hardening characteristic. Compared with the homogenized alloy, the HSLA magnesium alloy had a significantly higher cyclic stress level at all strain amplitudes, along with a longer fatigue life at lower and intermediate strain amplitudes owing to its higher monotonic strength. However, the homogenized alloy showed a longer fatigue life at a high strain amplitude of 0.8 % due to its better ductility and stronger capacity of storing deformation. While {10–12}<10−11> extension twinning occurred in both the homogenized and HSLA samples at high strain amplitudes, twins were primarily formed in the coarse unDRX grains in the compressive phase during cyclic deformation due to the c-axes of unDRX grains perpendicular to the loading direction, with twinning in the ultra-fine DRX grains being suppressed. The low-cycle fatigue life of both the homogenized and HSLA samples can be well predicted through an accumulative damage model based on the strain-energy density calculation and intrinsic fatigue toughness concept.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Due to the traits of low density, high specific strength and specific stiffness, etc., magnesium (Mg) alloys hold great promise in the realm of lightweight structural applications, such as in the automotive and aerospace industries [ 1 , 2 ]. However, the yield strength (YS) of most Mg alloys typically falls below 300 MPa  [3] . Extensive efforts, including grain refinement, alloying and texture modification, have been undertaken to enhance the mechanical properties of Mg alloys. For example, Wan et al.  [4]  achieved an impressive tensile yield strength (TYS) of 650 MPa in a Mg-8Gd-3Y-0.4Zr alloy with an average grain size of 80 nm by employing extrusion, rotary swaging, and aging processes. Besides, in the load-bearing structural applications, Mg alloys inevitably bear cyclic loading and thus fatigue fracture may occur. Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of cyclic deformation and fatigue behavior is imperative to ensure safety and reliability. Several researchers have conducted the investigation of strain-controlled low cycle fatigue (LCF) behavior of Mg alloys. Notably, an intriguing phenomenon has emerged wherein an asymmetry within the hysteresis loop between tensile and compressive reversals becomes evident, which is usually attributed to the activation of twinning-detwinning processes  [5] . It is reported that the LCF behavior is influenced by fatigue testing parameters, such as strain amplitude  [5–9]  and strain ratio [ 8 , 10 , 11 ] as well as strain rate [ 8 , 12 ] and microstructural factors (e.g., grain size  [12] , texture [ 5 , 13–15 ] and second-phase particles [ 16 , 17 ]). For structural materials, the desired properties encompass high strength, good ductility as well as superior LCF resistance. However, it is reported that a decrease in monotonic ductility corresponds to a reduction in LCF resistance  [18] , while the improvement of strength often correlates with a compromised ductility  [4] . Therefore, achieving high strength and high ductility as well as high LCF resistance simultaneously becomes a formidable challenge for Mg alloys.

Extrusion is widely employed to refine the coarse-grained microstructure of Mg alloys and thus improved mechanical properties can be obtained [ 19 , 20 ]. Besides, compared with high-alloyed Mg alloys, low-alloyed Mg alloys usually show good room-temperature ductility and formability due to the elimination of adverse effect of second-phase particles on deformation. However, the absence of effective strengthening phases presents a challenge in improving the strength of low-alloyed Mg alloys. In recent years, low-temperature/low-speed extrusion has emerged to be an effective method to improve the strength of low-alloyed Mg alloys. Zhang et al.  [21]  applied an extrusion temperature of 250 °C to treat Mg-0.8Zn-0.2Zr alloy, which exhibited a high TYS of 330 MPa, as well as a good elongation of 15.5%. Heterostructured materials have garnered significant interest owing to their outstanding mechanical properties [ 22 , 23 ]. It is noted that heterostructured Mg alloys consisting of fine DRX grains and coarse unDRX grains can be obtained at low extrusion temperature and/or low extrusion speed due to the inhibition of DRX. Therefore, hetero-deformation induced (HDI) strengthening also contributes to improving the strength due to the significant difference in microstructure (e.g., orientation and dislocation density) between the fine DRX grains and coarse unDRX grains  [24–26] . Previous research endeavors have been devoted to developing high-performance heterostructured Mg alloys while exploring the effect of microstructure on mechanical properties. Xiong et al.  [11]  studied the fatigue behavior of an extruded AZ31 alloy with coarse elongated grains and fine equiaxed grains, and reported that strong cyclic hardening was observed at a strain ratio of -∞. It is obvious that the application of heterostructured Mg alloys with superior mechanical properties also requires consideration of their fatigue behavior. However, there exists a notable gap in the understanding of the LCF behavior of low-temperature/low-speed extruded Mg alloys. Some important issues, such as cyclic straining/softening and fatigue life level relative to other Mg alloys, need to be identified. Besides, it is also necessary to clarify the applicability and accuracy of fatigue life prediction modeling in heterostructured Mg alloys.

Zn- and Ca-containing Mg alloys exhibit excellent biocompatibility and good mechanical properties [ 27 , 28 ], thus attracting a great deal of interest. However, the TYS of most extruded Mg-Zn-Ca alloys is in the range of 100–250 MPa [ 29 , 30 ]. The preparation of heterostructured Mg alloys enables the attainment of exceptional mechanical properties  [31–33] . A superior TYS of 406 MPa is achieved in a heterostructured Mg-2Zn-1.2Ca alloy via extrusion at a temperature of 250 °C with a low ram speed of 0.3 mm/s  [32] . Our previous work also showed that a low-alloyed Mg-Zn-Ca alloy extruded at 150 °C had a lamellar structure, which exhibited a superior TYS of 374 MPa and a good elongation of 14%. The reasons for the superior TYS were mainly attributed to the ultra-fine DRX grains, hard orientations, high-density dislocations and co-segregation of Zn and Ca atoms along grain boundaries. Besides, HDI strengthening also contributed to the improvement of TYS  [31] . In this work, to expand the lightweight structural application potential, the cyclic deformation behavior of the low-temperature extruded high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) Mg-Zn-Ca alloy was investigated via strain-controlled LCF tests. The fatigue life was predicted based on a strain-energy density approach, and different intrinsic fatigue toughness values were used to evaluate the accuracy of prediction. Besides, the effect of microstructure on the fatigue behavior was discussed, and the relationship between the tensile and fatigue properties was identified.

sections.heading: Materials and experimental procedure
paragraphs: The as-received Mg-1.2 wt.% Zn-0.1 wt.% Ca (ZX10) alloy was fabricated by semi-continuous casting. Homogenization was conducted at 375 °C for 24 h to dissolve the second-phase particles, thus ensuring the formability of subsequent low-temperature extrusion. Then the billet was extruded into cylinders with a diameter of 12 mm at 150 °C with an extrusion ratio of 17.4:1 and a ram speed of ∼2 mm/s. For the sake of convenience, the homogenized and extruded samples were subsequently labelled as Homo and ET150, respectively.

Optical microscopy (OM, VHX-600, Keyence, Japan) was used to observe the microstructure. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C Nano, Oxford Instruments, UK) in a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Gemini 300, Zeiss, Germany) was employed to characterize crystallographic orientation and examine the formation of twinning. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X, FEI, USA) was used to observe dislocations and fine precipitates in the extruded alloy. The dog-bone shaped fatigue samples with a gauge length of 16 mm, a width of 3 mm and a thickness of 3 mm were machined along the extrusion direction (ED) and then tested on an Instron 8801 fatigue testing system (Instron, Norwood, MA, USA) at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10 −2  s −1 , a constant strain ratio of −1 and different strain amplitudes (0.1%, 0.2%, 0.3%, 0.4%, 0.6% and 0.8%) in a strain control mode. At each strain amplitude, at least two samples were tested. After the number of cycles reached 10,000 at lower strain amplitudes, where the sample basically arrived at stabilization or saturation, stress control was applied with a sinusoidal waveform at a frequency of 50 Hz. Prior to testing, the surfaces of fatigue samples were ground with sandpapers up to grit 600. Also, the tensile properties were determined on a UTM5105 machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3  s −1  with dog-bone shaped samples with a gauge length of 15 mm, a width of 3 mm and a thickness of 2 mm machined along the ED.

sections.heading: Microstructure and tensile properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 1a 
                          shows a typical EBSD orientation map of Homo sample. It can be seen that the Homo sample exhibits basically random orientations with coarse grain sizes of ∼170 µm. The average basal Schmid factor with respect to the loading direction ( x -direction) is calculated to be ∼0.29 ( Fig. 1b ). After extrusion at 150 °C ( Fig. 1c ), the alloy exhibits a bimodal microstructure, with a fine DRX fraction of ∼67% measured via ImageJ software.  Fig. 1d  shows a basal Schmid factor map of ET150 sample with respect to the loading direction (ED). Different color codes represent different Schmid factor ranges. It can be seen that the unDRX coarse grains mainly show red color, which means that most of the unDRX grains have a lower basal Schmid factor (≤0.1), and also the  c -axes of unDRX grains are perpendicular to the ED. The statistical results show that the fractions of basal Schmid factor in the ranges of 0–0.1 and 0.1–0.2 are about 56.5% and 20.7%, respectively. Besides, the average basal Schmid factor is determined to be ∼0.14, which is lower than that of Homo sample (∼0.29), while the average DRX grain size is estimated to be ∼0.8 µm, as per the EBSD data. The TEM image ( Fig. 1e ) shows that the unDRX grains have high-density dislocations, and some fine precipitates can also be observed, as indicated by blue arrows. In  Fig. 1f , compared with Homo sample, ET150 sample shows a superior TYS of 374 MPa but a lower elongation of 14%. As summarized in an inserted graph in  Fig. 1f , the TYS of ET150 sample is superior to that of most extruded Mg-Zn-Ca alloys [ 29 , 30 , 32 , 34–40 ]. Meanwhile, it shows a good ductility compared with other high-strength Mg alloys (e.g., high-alloyed Mg-RE  [41–44]  and Mg-2Sn-2Ca  [45] ). Therefore, the present Mg-1.2 wt.% Zn-0.1 wt.% Ca alloy processed via a low-temperature extrusion at 150 °C can be referred to as a high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) magnesium alloy, being akin to the well-known HSLA steels in the area of ferrous alloys [ 46 , 47 ].

sections.heading: Low-cycle fatigue behavior
paragraphs:
Fig. 2a 
                          shows the typical stress-strain hysteresis loops of the first, second and mid-life cycles for Homo and ET150 samples tested at a strain amplitude of 0.8%. Compared with Homo sample, it can be seen that ET150 sample exhibits a higher cyclic stress. Besides, while Homo sample shows nearly symmetrical hysteresis loops, they are asymmetrical for ET150 sample.  Fig. 2b  and  c  shows the stress-strain hysteresis loops of mid-life cycles at different strain amplitudes for Homo and ET150 samples, respectively. In  Fig. 2b  (Homo sample), it is seen that the stress ratio (minimum cyclic stress/maximum cyclic stress) is determined to be about −1 at different strain amplitudes. In  Fig. 2 c (ET150 sample), the stress ratio is about −1 at strain amplitudes of ≤0.4%. However, the loops become asymmetrical at strain amplitudes of 0.6% and 0.8%, and the stress ratio decreases to about −0.76 at a strain amplitude of 0.8%, which indicates that yielding occurs earlier in compressive phase than that in tension at strain amplitudes of 0.6% and 0.8%. This deformation asymmetry was also observed by Begum et al.  [5]  and Lin and Chen  [13]  in an extruded AZ31 alloy, which was related to the Bauschinger effect and the activation of twinning during compression and detwinning during subsequent tension.

Fig. 3a 
                          presents the relationship between the stress amplitude and the number of cycles during cyclic deformation. It can be seen that ET150 sample shows a much higher cyclic stress amplitude at all strain amplitudes compared with Homo sample, especially at higher strain amplitudes of ≥0.3%. The higher cyclic stress of ET150 sample is related to its higher monotonic strength ( Fig. 1f ). At the low strain amplitudes (0.1% and 0.2%), the differences of stress amplitudes between Homo and ET150 samples become small. With increasing strain amplitude, the stress amplitude increases but results in a decrease in fatigue life for both Homo and ET150 samples. Besides, it is seen that the stress amplitudes are almost constant at strain amplitudes of ≤0.4% for ET150 sample, indicating the achievement of cyclic stabilization or saturation. However, at high strain amplitudes (0.6% and 0.8%), the stress amplitude increases with increasing number of cycles except for the first cycle, indicating that cyclic hardening occurs sequentially. Similar change was reported in extruded AZ31  [13]  and cast Mg-10Zn-5Al (ZA105)  [6]  alloys. In contrast, the stress amplitude increases with the number of cycles except for the strain amplitude of 0.1% for Homo sample. Moreover, the increased rate of stress amplitude correlating with rising strain amplitude in such a semi-logarithmic plot is higher in the Homo sample than in the ET150 sample. Such a cyclic hardening behavior has also been reported in other studies, such as Mg  [16]  and Al  [48]  alloys. It is known that the cyclic hardening or softening characteristics of materials are dependent on their composition, microstructure and initial state. Mirza et al.  [7]  reported that cyclic hardening occurred at the first three cycles followed by cyclic softening up to failure for strain amplitudes of 1.0% and 1.2%, and cyclic softening continued until fracture for strain amplitudes of 0.2–0.8% in a ME20 magnesium alloy processed by hot rolling and H112. It is reported that twinning, fine particles and dislocation pile-ups can hinder the movement of dislocations, thus leading to the cyclic hardening [ 5 , 13 , 49 , 50 ]. Also, the heterostructures in ET150 sample can cause dislocation accumulation at the interfaces of DRX/unDRX grains, thus generating back stresses to impede the further emission and movement of dislocations [ 22 , 23 ]. Cyclic softening could be induced by twinning in a cast AM50 alloy, possibly due to the reorientation of grains facilitating easy slip  [49] . Besides, dislocation annihilation and rearrangement would be one of the reasons for the cyclic softening  [51–53] . Cyclic stabilization or saturation would occur when the factors affecting cyclic hardening and cyclic softening reach an equilibrium.

The area of hysteresis loops represents the strain-energy density, which can be calculated via Matlab software.  Fig. 3b  shows the strain-energy density vs. the number of cycles in a double-log plot at different strain amplitudes. At lower strain amplitudes (0.1–0.3%), ET150 sample shows low plastic strain, resulting in unreliable hysteresis loop areas. Therefore, only strain amplitudes of 0.4–0.8% were used to calculate and compare the strain-energy density of both the Homo and ET150 samples. It can be seen that the strain-energy density of ET150 sample is lower than that of Homo sample at the same strain amplitude. Besides, the strain-energy density of ET150 sample shows a decreasing trend with increasing number of cycles until failure for strain amplitudes of 0.6% and 0.8%, while it shows a slightly increasing trend at the early stage of cyclic deformation for Homo sample.

Fig. 4a 
                          and  b  shows the change of loading elastic modulus with increasing number of cycles. For Homo sample ( Fig. 4a ), the elastic modulus keeps almost unchanged within the experimental scatter at a strain amplitude of 0.1%, while it shows an increasing trend with increasing number of cycles at strain amplitudes of 0.2–0.8%, which is related to pseudo-elasticity or non-linear elastic behavior [ 5 , 54 ]. Similar result was reported in cast ZA105  [6] , extruded AZ31 [ 5 , 13 ] and extruded AM30  [8]  alloys. The reasons for pseudoelasticity would be related to reversible movement of dislocations and twinning [ 5 , 8 , 55 ]. In contrast, the elastic modulus of ET150 sample is almost unchanged at all strain amplitudes due to the presence of abundant ultra-fine DRX grains ( Fig. 1c  and  d ). Non-basal dislocations, such as prismatic 〈a〉 and pyramidal <c+a> dislocations, might hinder the reversible movement of basal 〈a〉 dislocations and detwinning  [56] . In our previous work, non-basal dislocations have been reported in the extruded alloy  [31] . Also, non-basal dislocations can be activated during tensile and compressive deformation in fine-grained Mg-Zn-Ca alloys [ 24 , 57 ]. Therefore, it can be inferred that the disappearance of the pseudoelasticity in ET150 sample should be related to the behavior of non-basal dislocations along with the presence of ultra-fine DRX grains.

Fig. 5a 
                         - d  shows the fracture surfaces of Homo sample fatigued at a strain amplitude of 0.2%. Crack initiation, crack propagation and fast fracture can be observed on the fracture surface ( Fig. 5a ). The fatigue crack initiation occurs from the specimen surface.  Fig. 5b  shows the crack propagation region magnified from  Fig. 5a , where some fatigue striation features could be seen. Transgranular crack ( Fig. 5c ) and dimples ( Fig. 5d ) can be observed in the fast fracture region. The fracture surface of fatigued ET150 sample at a strain amplitude of 0.2% was also examined, as shown in  Fig. 5e – g . It is seen that the overall fracture surface is flatter compared with that of Homo sample ( Fig. 5a ). This is also attributed to the presence of ultra-fine DRX grains in the ET150 sample ( Fig. 1c  and  d ). Multiple crack initiation sites are observed to be near the specimen surface ( Fig. 5e ). Fatigue cracks with multiple directions (indicated by blue arrows) can be observed near the crack initiation site in  Fig. 5f .  Fig. 5g  is magnified from  Fig. 5e  in the crack propagation region, which shows the fatigue striations that are perpendicular to the crack growth direction.

sections.heading: Effect of microstructure on fatigue behavior
paragraphs:
It is noted that the microstructure and mechanical properties of Homo and ET150 samples are quite different ( Fig. 1 ). The main differences in microstructures lie in grain structure (homogeneous and heterogeneous), grain size, dislocation density and texture between Homo and ET150 samples. Intrinsic fatigue toughness ( W o 
                         ) signifies the fatigue damage capacity (somewhat like fracture toughness representing the fracture resistance in fracture mechanics), which corresponds to the ability to accommodate defects  [60] , and should be related to the microstructural characteristics. In this section, the effect of microstructure on the cyclic deformation behavior is discussed systematically.

He et al.  [16]  reported that the second phases could induce the formation of cracks, thus decreasing the fatigue resistance. The experimental material is a low-alloyed Mg alloy, and homogenization was conducted to dissolve the coarse second-phase particles prior to extrusion. Therefore, coarse particle-induced cracking can be ignored. Han et al.  [65]  reported that low recrystallized fractions (≤25 vol.%) decreased the fatigue life (≤8164 cycles) of heterostructured 316 L stainless steel. When the recrystallized fraction increased to 67 vol.%, the fatigue resistance was improved with a longer fatigue life of ∼13,400 cycles. The reason was that strain partitioning took place between hard and soft domains, and plastic strain was predominantly concentrated in the recrystallized grains. Besides, it is reported that strain transfer between fine DRX grains and coarse unDRX grains can alleviate local stress/strain concentration  [26] , while a low recrystallized fraction diminishes the capability to transfer dislocations  [25] , which would decrease the ductility and fatigue resistance. ET150 sample with a DRX fraction of 67% ( Fig. 1c ) exhibits a good elongation ( Fig. 1f ) and a high fatigue resistance ( Fig. 8 ), indicating that an effective combination of ultra-fine DRX grains and coarse unDRX grains is attained.

Fig. 9 
                          shows the EBSD results obtained from Homo and ET150 samples near the fracture regions under a strain amplitude of 0.8%. In  Fig. 9a , transgranular crack can be observed, as indicated by a yellow arrow. The red lines in  Fig. 9a  and  d  represent the boundaries with a misorientation of ∼86° In  Fig. 9b  and  e , it can be seen that the fractions of high-angle grain boundaries (>15°) for the Homo and ET150 samples are ∼73.2% and ∼75.0%, respectively. Also, obvious misorientation peaks around 86° can be observed in both the Homo and ET150 samples. This suggests that {10–12}<10−11> extension twins are activated during cyclic deformation. The formation of extension twins can also be confirmed from the misorientation line profiles along L1 and L2 ( Fig. 9c  and  F ). In the ET150 sample, the unDRX grains contain a high fraction of low-angle grain boundaries (white lines) indicating the formation of subgrains along with the ∼86° red lines. For Homo sample with coarse grains as well as random orientations ( Fig. 1a  and  b ), it is reasonable to infer that twins can be formed in both the compressive and tensile phases in the grains with favorable orientations relative to the loading direction. When the loading direction is reversed during cyclic deformation, detwinning occurs in the twinned grains and new twins may also form in the grains that are previously unfavorable for twin formation. This would be the reason for the nearly symmetrical hysteresis loops ( Fig. 2b ). It is clear that extension twinning occurs basically in the coarse unDRX grains in ET150 sample, which is absent in the ultra-fine DRX grain areas ( Fig. 9d – F ). It is known that the twin nucleation rate decreases with decreasing grain size, which is attributed to the sensitivity of twin nucleation stress to grain size  [66] . When the grain sizes are reduced to micron and submicron scales, the formation of twins is basically suppressed  [67] . Indeed, even in a dynamic compression process at high strain rates, a fine grain size of 3 µm was observed to be capable of inhibiting the twinning in a Mg-2Y-0.6Nd-0.6Zr alloy  [68] . Besides, the coarse unDRX grains of ET150 sample shows a preferential orientation with the  c -axes perpendicular to the loading direction ( Fig. 1d ), which are beneficial to activate extension twins in the compressive phase during cyclic deformation. In the tensile phase detwinning can occur [ 13 , 69–71 ]. Therefore, twinning-detwinning behavior occurs in the process of cyclic deformation, resulting in the presence of asymmetric hysteresis loop ( Fig. 2a ). The observation of twins in unDRX grains was also reported in an extruded Mg-5.2Zn-0.47Zr alloy via light microscope  [14]  and in an extruded Mg-1Zn-0.3Ca alloy via EBSD  [15] . Twins in the fcc metals can accommodate dislocation motion and relieve strain localization  [60] , while in hcp-Mg alloys twin boundaries could become crack initiation sites due to the strain/stress concentration, thus decreasing the fatigue resistance [ 15 , 53 ]. At low strain amplitudes, the low cyclic stress is insufficient to activate the twins, thus eliminating the possibility of twin boundaries becoming the crack initiation ( Fig. 2c ). Instead, dislocation slip induces crack formation  [72] . This transition in the deformation modes is advantageous for achieving a longer fatigue life  [53] . Also, the ultra-fine DRX grains can enhance the crack initial life  [73] , thus improving the fatigue resistance and leading to a longer fatigue life.

Mohammed et al.  [18]  investigated the cyclic deformation behavior of 2009Al alloy reinforced by carbon nanotube with a high TYS of 621 MPa and a low elongation of 2.6%, and observed that the higher strength was beneficial to achieve a superior fatigue life at lower strain amplitudes. However, the low ductility resulted in a decreased fatigue life at higher strain amplitudes. Mohammed et al.  [6]  further reported that a cast ZA105 alloy with a low elongation of 2.5% had a low fatigue life of ∼17 cycles at a strain amplitude of 0.8%, which was much lower than that of the Homo (∼536 cycles) and ET150 (∼176 cycles) samples. It is noted that ET150 sample shows a lower room-temperature ductility compared with Homo sample ( Fig. 1f ), which would be one of the reasons for the lower fatigue life of ET150 sample at the high strain amplitude of 0.8%. Besides, the energy generally accumulates quickly at high strain amplitudes, thus decreasing the fatigue life ( Figs. 3b  and  8 ). In  Fig. 3b , the strain-energy density of Homo sample increases first then keeps constant for strain amplitudes of 0.6% and 0.8%. However, the strain-energy density gradually decreases with increasing number of cycles for ET150 sample, indicating again the inadequate capacity of storing energy. In fact, Homo sample with coarse grain sizes can provide more space to accommodate strain during cyclic deformation compared with that of ET150 sample with ultra-fine DRX grains and high-density dislocations in unDRX grains ( Fig. 1a ,  d  and  e ). Therefore, the ability of storing deformation energy as well as the ductility play an important role in determining the fatigue life at high strain amplitudes. In  Fig. 6 , it can be seen that ET150 sample has a longer fatigue life at intermediate or lower strain amplitudes of 0.2%−0.4% compared with Homo sample. In this range of strain amplitudes, cyclic stabilization occurs in ET150 sample, while Homo sample still shows obvious strain hardening ( Fig. 3a ). Thus, the energy accumulation of Homo sample is more severe compared with ET150 sample. At the low strain amplitude of 0.1%, both Homo and ET150 samples are cyclic stable, and a long fatigue life of >10 7  cycles without failure is achieved. The reason is that the strain-energy density becomes increasingly lower for each hysteresis loop with decreasing strain amplitude in strain-controlled fatigue. This indicates that the sample can sustain more cyclic deformation, thus resulting in a longer fatigue life at lower strain amplitudes ( Fig. 6 ).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this work, a low-alloyed Mg-1.2Zn-0.1Ca alloy was extruded at 150 °C to achieve a unique heterostructure consisting of ultra-fine DRX grains and coarse unDRX grains with a high yield strength of 374 MPa along with an elongation of 14%, and strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue tests were performed on such a HSLA (high-strength low-alloy) magnesium alloy. The main conclusions can be drawn as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            The homogenized sample with a uniform coarse-grained microstructure exhibited symmetrical hysteresis loops, and obvious cyclic hardening was observed at all strain amplitudes except for the low strain amplitude of 0.1%. In contrast, the low-temperature extruded HSLA magnesium alloy with coarse unDRX grains and ultra-fine DRX grains of 0.8 µm showed asymmetrical hysteresis loops at high strain amplitudes of 0.6% and 0.8%, and cyclic softening occurred at the first cycle followed by cyclic hardening until failure. Besides, cyclic stabilization was achieved at strain amplitudes of ≤0.4%. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The HSLA sample showed a lower fatigue life at a high strain amplitude of 0.8% compared with the homogenized sample, which was related to its relatively lower ductility and limited dislocation storage capacity due to the ultra-fine grains and high-density dislocations in coarse unDRX grains. However, at intermediate and lower strain amplitudes (0.2%−0.4%), a longer fatigue life was attained in the HSLA sample due to its higher monotonic strength. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            {10–12}<10−11> extension twinning was observed in both the homogenized and HSLA samples during cyclic deformation. In the HSLA sample, twins were primarily formed in the coarse unDRX grains in the compressive phase during cyclic deformation due to the  c -axes of unDRX grains perpendicular to the loading direction, while the twinning in the ultra-fine DRX grains was suppressed. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The low-cycle fatigue life of homogenized and HSLA samples can be well predicted based on the strain energy-density and accumulative damage modal. For the homogenized sample, the predicted fatigue lives based on different intrinsic fatigue toughness ( W o 
                               ) values all show small differences compared with the experimental lives. For the HSLA sample, utilizing the  W o 
                                value derived from the consideration of all hysteresis loop areas from the first cycle to the sample failure can yield a more accurate fatigue life prediction.
